extracted.intended_audience: writers submitting short fiction to Clarkesworld Magazine or Neil Clarke–edited anthologies (slush/short story authors)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for what to include, omit, and how to format a cover letter (or 'relevant notes') when submitting short stories to Clarkesworld or Neil Clarke’s anthologies. Advises on disclosures (translations, minors, non-native speakers), formatting placement, rights, and common cover-letter anti-patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to address a cover letter
rubrics_metrics.description: Skip salutations like 'Dear Neil', 'Dear Mr. Clarke', 'Dear Editor' — they have no impact and simple mistakes can work against you.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Neil: 'Just skip the niceties and dive right into the substance.' Example of an anti-pattern: addressing the wrong editor (e.g., 'Dear Sheila') which implies you sent it elsewhere or reused the wrong letter. Editors vary in reaction (some hate it, some find it amusing), so avoid the risk by omitting formal salutations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep the cover letter very short
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer very short cover letters; if your cover letter is long (beyond the few positive reasons listed), you've likely done something wrong.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarkesworld enforces a 450 character limit on the cover letter in the submission system to push brevity. The editor reads cover letters last and aims for concise 'relevant notes' rather than long exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclose relevant professional or personal experience
rubrics_metrics.description: If a particular aspect of the story pulls from your professional (e.g., physicist, historian, astronaut, musician) or personal experience (cultural, regional, temporal), mention it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You don't have to 'write what you know', but if you do know something that informs authenticity, telling the editor may cause them to re-evaluate or read further. Treat this disclosure as potentially motivating the editor to re-check the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclose non-native English speaker status
rubrics_metrics.description: If you are a non-native English speaker, say so in the cover letter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Neil: he will cut non-native writers more slack on spelling and grammar and recognizes storytelling approaches may be non-standard. This is important for evaluation and editing phases. This disclosure can affect how strictly errors are judged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclose if you are under 18 (minor)
rubrics_metrics.description: If you are under 18, tell the editor in the cover letter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editor: impressed by young writers; will cut some slack on grammar/spelling. Practical impact: if accepted, a parent or legal guardian will be required to co-sign the contract (legal requirement).

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclose if previously unpublished / publication history
rubrics_metrics.description: If you are previously unpublished, you may mention it, but don't treat publication history as a selling point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Neil: 'I'm not buying names. I'm buying stories.' Editors like being first publishers for authors; telling them up-front helps avoid surprises. Anti-pattern: long 'laundry list' of every publication — never include more than three, and honestly better to omit publication credits altogether unless directly relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submitting a translation — required disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: When submitting a translation, state where the story was originally published (if it has been), the original language, your relationship to the story (author or translator), and whether you have approval of whoever holds the original rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translator's name should be in the manuscript (typically under the author's byline). Note that rights holders may not be the original author (could be estate/publisher), so clarify permission status. Provide original-publication details if applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submitting a reprint — required disclosures and policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Clarkesworld magazine does not accept reprints; for reprint anthologies Neil edits you must disclose where and when the story was originally published and any restrictions (time, region, or language).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a story has been previously published (even 'published badly'), it is treated as a reprint. Substantial changes would be required before most editors would consider it new. For Clarkesworld magazine specifically, do not submit reprints.

rubrics_metrics.name: If you aren't the author, state your relationship and permission
rubrics_metrics.description: If someone other than the author is submitting (agent, representative of an estate, translator), state that in the cover letter and be prepared for verification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legitimate reasons exist (agents, estate reps, translations). The publication will verify representation before issuing a contract. Anti-pattern: submitting without author permission — do not submit a story on someone else's behalf without their consent.

rubrics_metrics.name: If genre selection was 'other', explain which genre you think it is
rubrics_metrics.description: If you selected 'other' for genre (because it doesn't fit listed categories), explain what genre you consider it to be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This helps editors categorize works that don't fit standard genre boxes. Note: Clarkesworld no longer provides 'other' because of misuse, but if applicable, clarify the genre in the note.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not repeat information already provided in the submission form or manuscript
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't repeat title, genre, word count, email address, or other fields already captured by the submission system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The submission system asks for title/genre/word count/email; repeating them in the cover letter is pointless. Mailing address belongs on the first page of the manuscript, not the cover letter. Do not include phone numbers, bank/PayPal information, or other sensitive payment data in the cover letter. These are unnecessary and an anti-pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not include a summary of the story
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid giving a synopsis or blurb of the story in the cover letter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Neil: summaries are unnecessary and can be detrimental to evaluation; he reads the cover letter last and prefers the writing to speak for itself. Editors commonly advise against summaries for short fiction cover letters. If you want to draw interest, the manuscript itself should do that.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manuscript formatting and placement of contact/legal name and pseudonym
rubrics_metrics.description: Place contact information and legal name on the manuscript's first page (standard header), and put a pseudonym under the story title in the manuscript rather than in the cover letter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow standard manuscript formatting (Neil links to shunn.net formatting). He specifies the legal name/contact should be in the top left of the first page and the pen name under the title. The cover letter does not need to duplicate this information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include special formatting within the manuscript, not just the cover letter
rubrics_metrics.description: If special formatting (fonts, sections, a different font for a robot report, etc.) is part of the story, include it in the submitted manuscript.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You may optionally note such formatting in the cover letter, but the editor will see it in the manuscript before reading the letter. For small file-format constraints, note any conversion/format changes in submission notes if they might affect presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Withdrawal and resubmission policy / handling errors
rubrics_metrics.description: You may withdraw a submission by contacting the publication; resubmitted work will move to the back of the queue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minor spelling errors are not usually cause to withdraw; Neil: 'If it’s just a few spelling errors, I wouldn’t worry about it.' If you withdraw and resubmit, you'll lose your place in the slush reader queue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Machine translation is not permitted
rubrics_metrics.description: Machine translation (e.g., Google Translate) is not allowed even as a starting pass for translated submissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If translating, the work must be a human translation; machine-assisted drafts are disallowed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rights and audio/podcast terms relevant to submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Clarkesworld requires audio rights for stories (they podcast accepted stories) and holds exclusive rights to published works for six months from publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a story was previously published as a podcast (or elsewhere) such prior publication may preclude first-rights requirements. The audio edition produced by Clarkesworld cannot be repurposed by the author, though the author may create a new recording after exclusive period; linking to the published version is allowed. Note: rights terms affect submission eligibility (first rights/reprints).

rubrics_metrics.name: If none of the above disclosures apply, a brief thank-you suffices
rubrics_metrics.description: If you have none of the specific disclosures (translation, minor, non-native speaker, relevant professional background, reprint/translation/representation issues), a simple 'Thank you for considering my story' is more than enough.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Neil deliberately avoids providing a single template example because many valid brief approaches exist; the last-paragraph guidance (short, polite) is sufficient for most submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit publication credits; avoid a long 'laundry list'
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not include an exhaustive list of prior publication credits in the cover letter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you do mention credits, never include more than three. Better yet, omit publication histories entirely unless directly relevant. Editors prefer to read the story rather than be influenced by a long credits list.
